overview: Across the region now called Haiti, household objects and living traditions reveal food, work and creativity: Taíno cloth stamps, colonial kitchen pottery, family soup-making and metal sculpture. These examples belong to different communities and centuries.

periods.title: Taíno towns before European contact
periods.summary: En Bas Saline was a large Taíno town from around 1200. This selected site phase does not date the first settlement of Haiti or the beginnings of Taíno culture.

periods.title: Contact and colonial settlements
periods.summary: Columbus arrived in 1492, and Spanish colonization followed. Puerto Real, on the northern coast, existed from 1503 to 1578. Indigenous communities did not simply vanish at first contact.

periods.title: French Saint-Domingue
periods.summary: The Treaty of Ryswick formalized the French western and Spanish eastern division of Hispaniola in 1697. Saint-Domingue’s plantation society depended on slavery.

periods.title: Revolution and the struggle for freedom
periods.summary: The large uprising in northern Saint-Domingue in August 1791 became part of the revolution that ended French colonial rule.

periods.title: Independence under Dessalines
periods.summary: Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed independence on January 1, 1804. His rule ended with his death in 1806.

periods.title: Divided Haitian states
periods.summary: After Dessalines’s death, Haiti divided politically. Alexandre Pétion governed the south, while Henri Christophe ruled the north and became king in 1811. The 1815 map’s single outline hides this division.

periods.title: Reunification and recognition
periods.summary: Jean-Pierre Boyer reunited northern and southern Haiti in 1820 and extended rule across Hispaniola in 1822. The United States recognized Haitian independence in 1862. This broad phase contains further changes of government and territory.

periods.title: U.S. military occupation
periods.summary: U.S. forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, restricting its sovereignty. Their withdrawal ended that occupation.

periods.title: After the U.S. occupation
periods.summary: The occupation ended in 1934. The dated examples below follow later cultural creativity and community life; this broad phase does not imply one continuous government.

items.text: At En Bas Saline, archaeologists recovered fishing weights, cooking griddles, shell and bone tools, beads and stamps used to put patterns on cotton cloth. These objects come from a Taíno town occupied in the centuries around European contact. A patterned shirt has a history too: people cared about useful equipment and how things looked, long before machine-printed fabric.

Fish and shellfish supplied much of En Bas Saline’s animal food. Researchers found larger fish and a wider variety of animal remains in the central mound area than around the town’s edges. They interpret this as evidence that higher-status residents, probably chiefs, ate differently. Ancient dinner scraps can reveal inequalities that grand buildings alone cannot explain.

Excavations at sixteenth-century Puerto Real found kitchen vessels made in Indigenous and African traditions, alongside imported European goods. A clay griddle was used for manioc bread. The kitchens show how colonial food depended on knowledge from different communities, many of whose members worked under coercion. The people preparing a meal shaped its history as much as those owning the dining table.

Puerto Real’s household finds include gaming pieces, children’s toys, a jaw harp, needlework equipment and decorated book fasteners. These are unusually personal traces of leisure and learning. They mostly illuminate the better-documented Spanish households, however. A toy found in one home cannot tell us what every child owned, and the lives of poorer and enslaved residents are less visible in these excavations.

sections.title: Social life, freedom and practical engineering

items.text: In 1772, officials in Port-au-Prince prohibited nighttime dances called Kalendas by enslaved and free people of colour. The regulation reveals attempts to control social gathering as well as work. It records what authorities wanted to stop, rather than proving that people stopped dancing.

Haitian independence in 1804 was a victory over French colonial rule and slavery. Freedom still had to be defended in everyday work: the John Carter Brown Library’s exhibition explains that Louverture and several early Haitian governments imposed forced plantation labour. Ending legal slavery did not immediately give everyone the right to choose their work.

The early nineteenth-century Citadelle Henry needed more than cannon and thick walls. Its builders included channels and cisterns to supply and store water. The fortress was intended to protect the new country, and its water system helped support people inside it. Even a mountain stronghold needs the practical equivalent of remembering everyone’s water bottle.

Joumou soup brings pumpkin, vegetables and other ingredients into a dish shared on January 1, Haiti’s Independence Day, and at Sunday breakfast. UNESCO’s 2021 heritage account describes women organizing preparation and children helping with ingredients, alongside farmers and utensil-makers. The meal connects a household to a much wider circle of work and celebration. Families can have their own versions.

In a 2023 report from Port-au-Prince, Marie France Damas cooked soup while her husband took restaurant orders and her daughter chopped vegetables. The business helped pay for her children’s schooling. This is one family’s documented experience, showing how a cherished meal could support both household income and education.

Smithsonian’s 2022 account follows metalworker Josnel Bruno turning a discarded steel oil drum into a vase. He flattens the metal, draws his design, then cuts it with a chisel called a burin. Flowers, birds and fruit inspire his work in Croix-des-Bouquets. The old container gains a dramatically different job description: from industrial storage to handmade art.

sections.title: Learning, medicine and what happens after flushing

items.text: In October 2013, fourteen Haitian doctors began the first medical residencies at University Hospital in Mirebalais. Their training covered children’s medicine, internal medicine and surgery, with an hour of dedicated teaching each day alongside supervised clinical work. A teaching hospital is also a workplace where already-qualified doctors continue learning from more experienced colleagues.

A 2013 engineering report describes where that hospital’s toilet, sink and laundry water went: a treatment system using bacteria to break down organic waste, followed by chlorine disinfection. Flushing was only the start of the journey. The less glamorous parts of a hospital require skilled design too, even if the pipes rarely get a thank-you card.

ending.text: French colonial rule ended with Haitian independence in 1804. The map’s earlier 1783 endpoint is not that event. Later political changes did not end Haitian cultural life: family food traditions and creative work continue.
